title: Test out of Part B
crib:
These are the R behaviours the questions rely on. If you know another
language, check them — several differ from Python's pandas.

- **A data frame is a table**: one row per patient, one column per thing
  measured. Each column holds one type of value.
- **`df$col`** gives one column, as a vector.
- **`df[row, column]`** picks by row first, then column, counting from 1.
  Leave a side blank to get all of it: `df[3, ]` is the whole of row 3.
  Columns can be named in quotes: `df[, "sbp"]`.
- **`df[condition, ]`** keeps the rows where the condition is TRUE. If the
  condition is `NA` for a row, R doesn't drop it — you get a row of `NA`s.
  (pandas drops it.)
- **`&`** means *and*; **`|`** means *or*.
- **`nrow()`** counts rows. **`class()`** says what type something is:
  `"numeric"`, `"character"` (text) or `"logical"` (TRUE/FALSE).
- **`df$new <- values`** adds or replaces a column. It needs one value per
  row — or a single value, which fills every row.
- **`ifelse(test, yes, no)`** gives the `yes` value where the test is TRUE,
  and the `no` value where it's FALSE.
- Storing into one data frame never changes another, even one it was made
  from.
context:
Most questions use this data frame, called `patients`:

```
  age blood_type sbp discharged
1  67         A+ 142       TRUE
2  54         O- 118      FALSE
3  71         B+  NA      FALSE
4  48         O+ 131       TRUE
5  62         A- 156       TRUE
```

options.feedback:
Right. Patient 3's systolic is missing, and `mean()` won't guess, so
the result is `NA`. Adding `na.rm = TRUE` would leave the missing
value out.

That's the mean of the four readings you have. `mean()` only leaves
the missing one out if you ask it to, with `na.rm = TRUE`.

That treats the missing value as zero. R never does that: a missing
value isn't a zero, so the result is `NA`.

No error. `mean()` gives `NA`, R's way of saying the answer can't be
known from this data.

items.title: A column of text
items.prompt:
A lab column holds `"12.4"`, `"<5"` and `"31.0"`. What does
`class(labs$crp)` give?

options.feedback:
Right. A column holds one type, and `"<5"` can't be a number, so the
whole column is text — even the entries that look like numbers.
Arithmetic on it will fail or go quietly wrong until it's converted.

Two of the three look like numbers, but `"<5"` doesn't, and a column
holds only one type. So the whole column is text.

options.text: Two types — numeric for two values, character for one
options.feedback:
A column can hold only one type. One text entry makes the whole
column text.

Nothing is missing. All three entries are there; one of them simply
isn't a number, which makes the column text.

Right. Each TRUE counts as 1 and each FALSE as 0, so the sum is the
number of patients who went home.

That's the number of patients. FALSE counts as 0, so only the three
TRUEs add to the total.

That's the number still in hospital — the FALSEs. The sum counts the
TRUEs.

options.text: An error — you can't add TRUE and FALSE
options.feedback: You can. TRUE counts as 1 and FALSE as 0.
Right. Row first, then column: row 2, the `age` column.
That's row 1. R counts rows from 1, so row 2 is the second patient.

That's row 3. In R, row 2 is the second row, because counting starts
at 1.

That would be `patients[, "age"]`, with the row side left blank. Here
the row is 2.

Right. Row 3, and the column side is blank, which means all of the
columns: age, blood type, systolic and discharge, for one patient.

options.text: The third column, for every patient
options.feedback:
Rows come first. The 3 is in the row position, so it picks row 3. The
third column would be `patients[, 3]`.

options.text: An error — the column is missing
options.feedback:
A blank side isn't missing; it means *all*. Leaving the column side
blank gives every column.

You'd need to name the column for that: `patients[3, "age"]`. With
the column side blank, you get every column.

Right. `patients$discharged` is TRUE for patients 1, 4 and 5, so those
rows are kept, and the `age` column is taken from them.

Those are the patients still in hospital — the FALSEs. The rows kept
are the ones where the condition is TRUE.

The condition goes in the row position, so only the rows where it's
TRUE are kept.
That's how many patients went home. This gives their ages.

items.title: A filter and a missing value
items.prompt:
Patient 3's systolic is missing. How many rows does this give?

```r
nrow(patients[patients$sbp > 140, ])
```

options.feedback:
Right — and this is the one that catches people. Two patients are over
140. For patient 3, `NA > 140` is `NA`, and R doesn't drop that row:
it adds a row of `NA`s. So you get three rows, one of them a patient
who doesn't exist.

Two patients really are over 140, and pandas would give 2. But R
handles the missing value differently: a condition that's `NA` gives
a row of `NA`s, so there are three rows.

Both 142 and 156 are over 140, so at least two rows are kept — and
the missing value adds a third.

No error. R quietly adds a row of `NA`s for the missing value, which
is what makes it dangerous.

items.title: Two conditions at once
items.prompt:
What does this give?

```r
patients[patients$age > 60 & patients$discharged, "age"]
```

options.feedback:
Right. Both conditions must be TRUE. Three patients are over 60 —
67, 71 and 62 — and of those, 67 and 62 went home.

Those are everyone over 60. `&` also needs `discharged` to be TRUE,
and the 71-year-old hasn't gone home.

Those are everyone who went home. `&` also needs the age to be over
60, which rules out the 48-year-old.

That's everyone who meets *either* condition — what `|` would give.
`&` needs both.

options.text: An error — three values for five rows
options.feedback:
Right. A new column needs one value per row, or a single value to fill
them all. Three values for five patients would pair readings with the
wrong people, so R stops.

options.text: The three values fill the first three rows; the rest are NA
options.feedback:
R won't guess which patients the values belong to. It stops with an
error instead.

options.text: The three values repeat to fill all five rows
options.feedback:
R repeats a *single* value, but not three across five rows: that would
pair readings with the wrong patients. It stops with an error.

options.text: The data frame is cut down to three rows
options.feedback:
Adding a column never removes rows. R stops with an error because the
lengths don't match.

items.title: One value for every row
items.prompt:
```r
patients$checked <- TRUE
```

What is in the new `checked` column?

options.feedback: Right. A single value fills every row.

options.text: TRUE for the first patient; NA for the rest
options.feedback: A single value isn't placed in one row. It fills all of them.

options.text: An error — one value for five rows
options.feedback:
One value is allowed: it fills every row. The error comes when there
are several values that don't match the number of rows.
It's stored, in every row of the new column.

items.title: Labels from a condition
items.prompt:
```r
patients$group <- ifelse(patients$age >= 65, "under 65", "65 and over")
```

What label does the 67-year-old get?

options.feedback:
Right — and it's wrong. The test is TRUE for a 67-year-old, so they
get the first label, `"under 65"`. The labels are in the wrong order:
the code runs without complaint, and every patient is mislabelled.

That's the label they *should* get. But `ifelse()` gives the first
label where the test is TRUE, and the first label written here is
`"under 65"`.

The 67-year-old's age isn't missing, so they get a label: the first
one, because the test is TRUE.

options.text: An error — the labels are the wrong way round
options.feedback:
R can't know the labels are the wrong way round. It gives the first
label where the test is TRUE, without complaint.

items.title: A change on a copy
items.prompt:
```r
older <- patients[patients$age > 60, ]
older$flag <- TRUE
```

Does `patients` now have a `flag` column?

options.feedback:
Right. `older` is a separate data frame made from `patients`. Storing
into it never changes `patients`.

`older` was made from `patients`, but it's separate. Changing it
leaves `patients` exactly as it was.
Nothing was stored into `patients`. Only `older` gained the column.
No error. `older` gets the new column; `patients` is untouched.
